gems_intro:
A Ruby virtual machine is only useful with a library around it, so each gem the
ecosystem needs is reimplemented in pure Go in its own `go-ruby-*` organisation:
the standard library, Rails and its dependencies, the testing stack, the Puppet
stack, database drivers, serialisation formats and template engines.

Every one of them is byte-compared against MRI where a byte comparison is
meaningful — a checksum, a `Marshal` payload, a formatted number. Where it is not
(a deflate stream, say, whose output is implementation-defined) the requirement is
interoperability in both directions instead.

Two things to know before reaching for one:

- **The gem organisation is the Ruby-facing wrapper, not always the engine.** Some
  are thin shells over an engine that lives in its own non-Ruby organisation — the
  regexp gem wraps [`go-regexp/engine`](https://github.com/go-regexp/engine), the
  sass gem wraps [`go-scss/scss`](https://github.com/go-scss/scss). If you are
  writing Go rather than Ruby, take the engine.
- **The repository inside is named after the gem**, not after the organisation:
  `go-ruby-activerecord/activerecord`.

families.title: Desktop & widgets
families.blurb: One widget toolkit, every surface it paints on, and the platform plumbing a real desktop needs.

orgs.role: GTK4 driven from pure Go over purego, CGO=0 — the Linux native-toolkit bridge for go-widgets, sibling of go-macos/objc.

The widget toolkit and every surface it paints on: the painter seam, MVVM, a declarative skin engine, a terminal back-end, a native window on X11, Wayland, Cocoa and Win32, application lifecycle with a system tray, a real Android APK, and a desktop shell.

freedesktop.org integration — .desktop entries, icon themes, shared MIME info, application associations, the menu tree, desktop notifications and Secret Service — over an owned X11 protocol core that also serves screen capture and the toolkit's window back-end.

Icon and logo packs as embedded pure-Go SVG data — Simple Icons brand marks, Devicon, Material and Seti file types, vscode-icons, and Iconoir. One repository per pack, so a program embeds the set it draws and not the other five; the drawing itself is go-gfx's `svg` package.
The freedesktop Thumbnail Managing Standard cache.
One secret store over macOS Keychain, Windows Credential Manager and Linux Secret Service — no cgo, no CLI exec.

The macOS foundation, all of it CGO-free through purego: the shared Objective-C runtime bridge, real AppKit controls embedded in a Go-painted window, Keychain and Touch ID, notifications and menu-bar items, accessibility, global hotkeys, login items and launch agents, IOKit HID, DiskArbitration, hardware audio and video decode, ScreenCaptureKit capture, and virtual displays the desktop extends onto.
The Windows foundation: Win32 bindings and WinRT interop on combase — peer of go-macos/objc — plus DXGI Desktop Duplication and GDI screen capture built on them.
A desktop in the browser — a Wayland-inspired compositor and window manager, a dock, a login portal, OCI app packaging and a coreutils suite.
Linux's system interfaces in pure Go: hidraw and the authentication factors built on it — the Linux third of the platform layer, beside go-macos and go-mswin.
Proving a person is present: the FIDO client-to-authenticator protocol spoken to a security key on any OS, and the rule that decides whether enough factors answered.
A menu-bar application on the toolkit: AI usage quotas across several accounts, read through one go-plugin contract with a plugin per provider.

families.title: Graphics, images & media
families.blurb: The 2D socle everything above draws through, and the pixels and frames it moves.

orgs.role: The shared 2D socle: an anti-aliased vector rasteriser, a raster surface, colour, geometry, resampling, and SVG to bitmap.
Image processing at scikit-image scope.
An audio/video toolkit — MP4/ISO-BMFF and Matroska/WebM demuxing.
Site-agnostic transport for streaming media: a retrying, rate-limited HTTP client, an HLS parser and an MPEG-DASH manifest reader.
A plugin framework for media extractors — standalone plugin executables answer what is at a URL and what can be downloaded from it.

XR glasses: head orientation, stereo frame packing, flat, equirectangular and fisheye projection, a 360° screen ribbon, a graded catalogue of what each headset can show — plus a player, a virtual desktop on the ribbon, and Android capture.

families.title: Documents, typesetting & fonts
families.blurb: Turning a document into pages: fonts, breaking, shaping, TeX, PDF, and one rich-document model.

orgs.role: A TeX engine — mouth and gullet, math mode to SVG, a PDF-figure rasteriser, and a fetcher that gets a document the class files it asks for without redistributing any.
The typesetting algorithms on their own, with no TeX vocabulary in the API: Knuth-Plass line breaking, Liang hyphenation, the Unicode bidirectional algorithm.
The font format: TrueType/OpenType parsing and anti-aliased rasterisation, a HarfBuzz-lite complex-text shaper, and legible fonts ready to import.
TeX's SyncTeX — the source-to-PDF correspondence, both ways.

The PDF stack, both directions: a 1.7 writer with TrueType and CFF subsetting, a reader and renderer, AcroForm and XFA form fields, text and structure extraction, a conformance suite judged against poppler, and a co-editable reader application built on all of it.

reStructuredText both ways: docutils' core in pure Go — the parser and the doctree the LaTeX and PDF path is built on — and an extractor that renders a Go package's own API documentation as reST to feed it.
One rich-document model, and the converters that read and write it — Markdown, LaTeX and reStructuredText.
OpenDocument Text, in and out of the richdoc model.
RTF, in and out of the richdoc model.

families.title: Markup, templating & text
families.blurb: Reading and writing the formats documents arrive in, and the engines that scan them.

orgs.role: Strict CommonMark 0.31.2 to HTML — all 652 spec examples.
kramdown-flavoured Markdown, as Jekyll uses it.
HTML and XML: parse, query, mutate, serialise.
XSLT transformation.
A Sass/SCSS compiler with Dart-Sass-compatible output — the engine behind the Ruby sass gem.
Logic-less Mustache templating, spec-faithful.
Shopify's Liquid template engine, gem-faithful.
A Rouge/Pygments-class syntax highlighter — per-language lexers, token types, named themes.
An Onigmo engine shaped like the standard library's regexp, with the lookaround and backreferences RE2 cannot do.
A lenient parser for the dates people actually write.

families.title: Web & transports
families.blurb: Rendering a page without a browser, and carrying gRPC where gRPC does not go.

orgs.role: A headless web engine: HTML and CSS laid out and painted to an image, with no Chromium — plus a service that streams those frames to a thin client.
An http.Client that presents a Chrome TLS fingerprint.
A WebSocket-to-stdio bridge for JSON-RPC language-server traffic.
gRPC where it is not supposed to go: over SSH, WireGuard, vsock, WebSocket and WebRTC.

families.title: Realtime collaboration
families.blurb: Many people, one document, no server deciding who won.

orgs.role: A replicated text document and the service that carries it between the people editing it — the same merge logic on the server and in the browser, via js/wasm.
A Yjs y-websocket relay hub, transport-agnostic.

families.title: Ruby, in Go
families.blurb: A Ruby virtual machine, its object model, and one organisation per gem it needs.

orgs.role: The Ruby virtual machine — YARV bytecode, the object model, the core library, and the rbgo interpreter.
Ruby's numeric tower, collections, time and dates as composition-oriented building blocks: Result-based, Null-Object, never nil.
MVVM, widgets and a terminal toolkit, addressable from Ruby.
go vet analyzers that make the ecosystem's invariants a compile-time matter.

families.title: CPU, SIMD & numerics
families.blurb: Getting the machine's width out of pure Go, on all six 64-bit targets.

orgs.role: Ergonomic generation of Go-compatible Plan 9 assembly for every 64-bit Go target.
SIMD kernels on all six of Go's 64-bit targets — codecs, hashes, string scans, bitsets, float and int8 dot products.
A numpy-shaped n-dimensional array, with GEMM at vecLib parity.
Fast Fourier transforms at numpy and scipy accuracy, without FFTW.

families.title: Compression, delta & erasure
families.blurb: Making bytes smaller, sending only what changed, and surviving what is lost.

orgs.role: LZFSE, LZ4, deflate and BLAKE3, with the CLIs that go with them.
Delta transfer: zsync2, rdiff, zchunk, vcdiff, bita — and the one content-defined chunker they all import.
Erasure coding: Reed-Solomon over GF(2^16), and the Mojette transform.

families.title: Storage, volumes & filesystems
families.blurb: From a block device to a mounted filesystem, without a C library anywhere.

orgs.role: The block layer — a device contract, NBD, pools, replicas, S3, an OCI image as a block device, GPT and MBR, and parse-hardening guards.

Filesystem-format drivers — ext4, xfs, btrfs, zfs, apfs, ntfs, exfat, fat32, iso9660, squashfs and more — plus UEFI variable management and a format prober. And the other direction: NFSv3, SFTP and WebDAV servers that export any of them, so an image can be mounted by the host rather than only read by a program.
Disk-image formats: qcow2, raw, dmg, tart-oci, in either direction.
Linux kernel ioctl wrappers — zfs, btrfs, loop, device-mapper, block, copy-on-write clones.
Full-disk encryption: LUKS, APFS, and the plumbing that opens them.
The modes underneath: CCM, XTS, ZFS crypto.

families.title: Firmware, boot & trust
families.blurb: What runs before the kernel, and how you prove what ran.

orgs.role: TPM 2.0 end to end: transports, the command layer, EFI_TCG2, measured boot, event-log replay and remote attestation.
PE/COFF for UEFI — an object-to-EFI linker, a signing and conversion CLI, and a self-extracting EFI packer.
GRUB and systemd-boot tooling, composed on the storage, UEFI and TPM stacks rather than reimplementing them.
Booting the machine: a TamaGo UEFI payload, a unified kernel image, an init, kernels, ISOs, SEV-SNP.
A minimal container host — OCI initrd and PXE boot, a DNS daemon, an OpenPubKey agent.

families.title: Packaging & supply chain
families.blurb: Building every dependency from source, signing it, and saying where it came from.

orgs.role: A pure-Go pkgx: the package manager, the bottle installer, the bk recipe builder, and the CI factory that publishes signed bottles.
SPDX and CycloneDX SBOMs, SLSA provenance, and Ed25519 signing that is minisign- and cosign-interoperable from one keypair.
Loose, pkgx-compatible semantic versions and ranges, CalVer included.

Guards on what leaves a machine: a global git hook that refuses a credential in a remote URL and a write to the branch pull requests land on, a credential helper that never lets a token reach a command line, and a scope checker that reads a token's powers without printing it.

families.title: Virtualisation, cloud & network
families.blurb: microVMs, guest drivers, supervision, coordination and the network between them.

orgs.role: weft — a Go-native microVM cloud: drivers, network, block storage, HA services, runners, clients, native apps, and the loom editor built on it.
Guest virtio drivers: net, blk, gpu with virgl and Venus, console, rng, vsock, balloon, fs, sound, input.
A PID-1 subreaper and process supervisor, and the restart state machine that decides when to try again.
Cross-host coordination on etcd v3: host liveness, watches, leader election.
A dependency-free DHCPv4 server library.
Active health probes — stateless TCP and HTTP checks folded into a rolling verdict.
VM pool management.
A WireGuard VPN with OIDC: the server, the client, and desktop apps for macOS, Linux and Windows.

families.title: Configuration management
families.blurb: The Puppet and Ansible stacks, in Go, without a Ruby or Python runtime.

orgs.role: The Puppet language and its catalogue compiler.
Puppet's Pcore type system: type calculus, parser, value model, assignability lattice.
PuppetDB.
Bolt — task and plan orchestration over SSH and WinRM.
Fact collection.
Hierarchical data lookup.
eyaml — encrypted values inside Hiera data.
HOCON configuration.
The Augeas engine: a config tree, path expressions and lenses.
Ansible: inventory, variable precedence, Jinja2-compatible templating, connection and become plugins, the module protocol, and the playbook engine.
The layer both orchestrators run commands through: local, SSH and WinRM connections with sudo, su and doas escalation.

families.title: News, social & feeds
families.blurb: One reader, and a client per source it reads.

orgs.role: A multi-source news and social aggregator with a go-widgets interface — Reddit, RSS, Hacker News, Usenet, Mastodon, Lemmy, Bluesky and more in one reader.
RSS, Atom and JSON Feed: parse and fetch.
Usenet, whole: NNTP, yEnc, Newznab, NZB, PAR2.
A Reddit read client, and a reader built on it.
A Mastodon read client.
A Lemmy read client.
A Hacker News read client.
A Bluesky / AT Protocol read client.
A best-effort read client for public Twitter/X timelines.
A best-effort read client for public Instagram profiles.
A best-effort read client for public TikTok profiles.

families.title: Games
families.blurb: Two engines hand-ported to pure Go, one of them onto bare metal.

orgs.role: Quake 1, hand-ported from tyrquake, with a bare-metal target.
DOOM, hand-ported through the gore lineage, with a TamaGo bare-metal back-end.

families.title: The map itself
families.blurb: The one thing this organisation does hold: the tool that generates every page here.

orgs.role: The generator. It reads the live GitHub organisation list and reconciles it against a curated classification, then writes the landing configuration, the family pages, the gem list and this profile. The reconciliation is the point: an organisation that holds code but is in no family fails the build, so the index cannot quietly omit something that exists.

readme_intro: # go-desktop **A map of one pure-Go ecosystem — {{summary}}, no C anywhere.** This organisation holds no library. It holds the index — and the tool that generates it, so that no number on any of these pages is typed by hand. Every library in the map is written in Go and compiled with `CGO_ENABLED=0`. That is not a stylistic preference: it is what makes one binary cross-compile to six architectures, run inside a browser as WebAssembly, and boot on bare metal without a libc. Where a good pure-Go library already exists it is used rather than rewritten; where the only option was a C library behind cgo, the capability was rebuilt. The ecosystem is split into **one organisation per domain and one repository per capability**, so a program that needs an ext4 reader takes an ext4 reader and not a storage framework. 🌐 **[go-desktop.github.io](https://go-desktop.github.io/)** — the same map, browsable · 📚 **[Documentation](https://go-desktop.github.io/docs/)** — with a [capability lookup](https://go-desktop.github.io/docs/latest/finding/): what you need, and the module that already does it.
readme_standards:
| | |
| --- | --- |
| **`CGO_ENABLED=0`** | No cgo, and no shelling out to a command-line tool in place of a library. A dependency is a Go module or it is written. |
| **Six 64-bit targets** | amd64, arm64, riscv64, loong64, ppc64le, s390x — native where runners exist, under qemu-user otherwise. s390x is big-endian, which keeps every on-disk and on-wire encoding honest. |
| **100% statement coverage** | A CI gate, error branches included. A skipped test is not a passing one: jobs fail when a toolchain is missing rather than turning green quietly. |
| **Measured, not asserted** | Performance claims come with a benchmark against the reference implementation; format claims come with a byte comparison against it. Decoders are fuzzed. |
| **One landing, one docs site** | A Hugo landing at `<org>.github.io` and versioned MkDocs Material docs at `<org>.github.io/docs/`, same brand, light/dark/system theme toggle. |
| **BSD-3-Clause** | Every repository, every organisation. |
reserved_intro:
These organisation names are reserved and empty. They are listed so the map has no
silent gaps: an empty organisation is not a shipped one, and a name that looks like
a capability is the easiest way to believe a capability exists.

# The pure-Go ecosystem

**{{orgs}} organisations. {{repos}} public code repositories. No C anywhere.**

`go-desktop` holds no library. It holds the index — a way to find a capability
without already knowing which organisation owns it — and
[the tool](https://github.com/go-desktop/catalog) that generates it, so that no
number on these pages is typed by hand.

Every library in the map is written in Go and compiled with `CGO_ENABLED=0`. That
is not a stylistic preference. It is what makes one binary cross-compile to six
architectures, run inside a browser as WebAssembly, and boot on bare metal without
a libc — three things a single cgo dependency takes away permanently.

## How the map is organised

**One organisation per domain, one repository per capability.** A program that
needs an ext4 reader takes an ext4 reader, not a storage framework. This is why
there are {{orgs}} organisations rather than a handful of monorepos: the unit of reuse
is the capability, and a capability that lives in its own module can be depended
on without dragging in the rest of its family.

The consequence to be aware of is that the map itself has to be maintained — which
is what this site is for. Before building anything, look here first: the recurring
failure mode in an ecosystem this wide is rebuilding something that already exists
one organisation over.

## Where to start

- **[Find a capability](finding.md)** — a lookup from what you need to where it lives.
- **[What every repository is held to](standards.md)** — the conformance standard, in full.
- The {{families}} families, in the navigation on the left.
- **[Ruby gems](gems.md)** — the {{gems}} per-gem organisations, alphabetically.
- **[Held, not yet built](reserved.md)** — the names that are held but hold nothing.

## Reading a count

Every repository count on this site is the number of **public repositories that
hold code**. The four infrastructure repositories every organisation carries —
`.github`, `brand`, `docs` and `<org>.github.io` — are excluded, because counting
them would inflate a one-library organisation to five.

Counts were measured against the live GitHub organisation list rather than
recalled, and the generated pages carry no hand-typed numbers.
